metadata.title: Slow motion of particle systems as a limit of a reaction-diffusion equation with half-Laplacian in dimension one

nodes.name: One-dimensional half-Laplacian operator $L$ (L\'evy-Khintchine formula)
nodes.statement: Let us set the one-dimensional half-Laplacian operator $L$ defined on functions $w\in L^\infty (\R)\cap C^{1,\beta}_{loc}(\R)$ for some $0<\beta<1$ by the L\'evy-Khintchine formula $$Lw(x)=\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{\R}\frac{dz}{z^2}\left(w(x+z)-w(x)-zw'(x) 1_{\left\{|z|\le 1\right\}}\right).$$
nodes.statement_short: The half-Laplacian $L$ on $\R$ written as a singular integral against the L\'evy measure $dz/z^2$.
nodes.genus: operator $L$ defined on functions $w\in L^\infty (\R)\cap C^{1,\beta}_{loc}(\R)$

nodes.name: Peierls-Nabarro layer-solution problem
nodes.statement: \left\{\begin{array}{l} L\phi -W'(\phi)=0 \quad \mbox{on}\quad \R,\\ \displaystyle{\phi'>0 \quad \mbox{and}\quad \phi(-\infty)=0,\quad \phi(0)=\frac 1 2,\quad \phi(+\infty)=1.} \end{array}\right.
nodes.statement_short: Stationary layer equation $L\phi=W'(\phi)$ with an increasing transition profile from $0$ to $1$.

nodes.name: Evolution equation for the Peierls-Nabarro model
nodes.statement: v_t=Lv-W'(v) + \sigma^\varepsilon(t,x) \quad \mbox{on}\quad (0,+\infty)\times \R
nodes.statement_short: Reaction-diffusion equation with half-Laplacian driven by an exterior stress.

nodes.name: Rescaled evolution problem for $v^\varepsilon$
nodes.statement: \left\{\begin{array}{l} \displaystyle{v^\varepsilon_t=\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\left\{Lv^\varepsilon-\frac{1}{\varepsilon}W'(v^\varepsilon) + \sigma(t,x)\right\} \quad \mbox{on}\quad (0,+\infty)\times \R}\\ \\ v^\varepsilon(0,x)=v^\varepsilon_0(x) \quad \mbox{for}\quad x\in\R. \end{array}\right.
nodes.statement_short: The $\varepsilon$-rescaled Cauchy problem whose singular limit is studied.

nodes.name: ODE system of particles with two-body $1/x$ interaction
nodes.statement: \left\{\begin{array}{lcl} \displaystyle{\frac{dx_i}{dt}}= \gamma \left(-\sigma(t,x_i) + \frac{1}{\pi}\sum_{j\not= i} \frac{1}{x_i-x_j}\right),\quad \mbox{on}\quad (0,+\infty),\\ x_i(0)=x_i^0, \end{array}\right| \quad \mbox{for}\quad i=1,...,N
nodes.statement_short: Limit dynamics: each particle moves under the exterior stress plus $1/\pi$ times the sum of $1/(x_i-x_j)$ interactions.

nodes.name: Mobility constant $\gamma$
nodes.statement: \gamma = \left(\int_{\R}(\phi')^2\right)^{-1}.

nodes.name: Assumption (A) i) on the potential $W$
nodes.statement: \noindent {\bf i) Assumption on the potential}\\ $$\left\{\begin{array}{l} W\in C^{2,\beta}(\R) \quad \mbox{for some}\quad 0<\beta<1,\\ \\ W(v+1)=W(v) \quad \mbox{for any}\quad v\in\R,\\ \\ W=0 \quad \mbox{on}\quad\Z,\\ \\ W>0 \quad \mbox{on}\quad\R\backslash \Z,\\ \\ W''(0)>0. \end{array}\right.$$
nodes.statement_short: $W$ is $C^{2,\beta}$, $1$-periodic, vanishes exactly on $\Z$, is positive elsewhere, and non-degenerate at $0$.

nodes.name: Assumption (A) ii) on the exterior stress $\sigma$
nodes.statement: \noindent {\bf ii) Assumption on the exterior stress} $$\left\{\begin{array}{l} \sigma \in BUC\left([0,+\infty )\times \R\right) \quad \mbox{and for some}\quad 0<\beta<1 \quad \mbox{and}\quad K>0, \quad \mbox{we have}\\ \\ |\sigma_x|_{L^\infty ([0,+\infty )\times \R)}\le K, \quad |\sigma_t|_{L^\infty ([0,+\infty )\times \R)}\le K,\\ \\ |\sigma_x(t,x+h)-\sigma_x(t,x)|\le K |h|^\beta \quad \mbox{for all}\quad x,h\in\R,\quad t\in [0,+\infty ). \end{array}\right.$$ We recall that BUC is the space of bounded uniformly continuous functions.
nodes.statement_short: $\sigma$ is bounded uniformly continuous with bounded Lipschitz derivatives and H\"older-continuous $\sigma_x$.

nodes.name: Assumption (A) iii) on the initial condition
nodes.statement: \noindent {\bf iii) Assumption on the initial condition} \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{array}{l} \mbox{For}\quad x_1^0< x_2^0< ...<x^0_N, \quad \mbox{we set}\\ \\ \displaystyle{v_0^\varepsilon(x)=\frac{\varepsilon}{\alpha}\sigma(0,x) + \sum_{i=1}^N \phi\left(\frac{x-x_i^0}{\varepsilon}\right) \quad \mbox{with}\quad \alpha=W''(0)>0.} \end{array}\right. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Initial datum is a stress-shifted superposition of $N$ ordered transition layers.

nodes.name: Theorem 1.1 (Convergence to the ODE system)
nodes.statement: {\bf (Convergence to the ODE system)}\\ Under assumption (A), there exists a unique solution $(x_i(t))_{i=1,...,N}$ of (\ref{eq::2}). Let $$v^0(t,x)= \sum_{i=1}^N H(x-x_i(t))$$ where $H(x)=1_{[0,+\infty)}(x)$ is the Heaviside function. Then for any $\varepsilon >0$, there exists a unique viscosity solution $v^\varepsilon$ of (\ref{eq::1}). Moreover as $\varepsilon \to 0$, $v^\varepsilon$ converges to $v^0$ in the following sense: \begin{equation} \limsup_{(t',x')\to(t,x),\ \e\to 0} v^{\e}(t',x')\leq (v^0)^* (t,x) \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \liminf_{(t',x')\to(t,x),\ \e\to 0} v^{\e}(t',x')\geq (v^0)_* (t,x) \end{equation} for $(t,x)\in [0,+\infty )\times \R$.
nodes.statement_short: As $\varepsilon\to0$ the solution of the rescaled PDE converges (in the half-relaxed-limit sense) to a sum of Heaviside steps moving by the particle ODE system.
conclusions: there exists a unique solution $(x_i(t))_{i=1,...,N}$ of (\ref{eq::2})
for any $\varepsilon >0$, there exists a unique viscosity solution $v^\varepsilon$ of (\ref{eq::1})

nodes.name: Remark 1.2 (semi-continuous envelopes)
nodes.statement: We recall here that the semi-continuous envelopes of a given any function $u$ are defined as follows $$u^*(t,x)=\limsup_{(t',x')\to(t,x)} u(t',x')\quad\quad\mbox{and}\quad\quad u_*(t,x)=\liminf_{(t',x')\to(t,x)} u(t',x').$$

nodes.name: Ansatz $\tilde{v}^\varepsilon$ for sub/supersolutions
nodes.statement: \tilde{v}^\varepsilon(t,x)=\frac{\varepsilon}{\alpha}\sigma(t,x)+\sum_{i=1}^N \left\{ \phi\left(\frac{x-x_i(t)}{\varepsilon}\right)-\varepsilon \dot{x}_i(t)\ \psi\left(\frac{x-x_i(t)}{\varepsilon}\right) \right\}
nodes.statement_short: Superposition of translated layers corrected at order $\varepsilon$ by the corrector $\psi$ and the stress.

nodes.name: Alberti-Bouchitt\'e-Seppecher singular-perturbation / Gamma-convergence result
nodes.statement: They have shown in \cite{Alberti-Bouchitte-Seppecher:singular-perturbations} that if we consider the energy functional for $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ and a double well potential $W$ given by $$E_\e[u]=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega} \abs{\nabla u}^2+\frac{1}{\e}\int_{\partial\Omega}W(u)$$ then, in particular, the rescalings $E_\e[u]/\abs{\log\e}$ Gamma-converge when $\e\to 0$ to $\frac{2}{\pi}\mathcal H^0(S_{u_0})$ if $n=2$ (thus $\partial\Omega$ is one dimensional) and the minimizers $u_\e$ converge to $u_0$, where $u_0=0,1$ on $\partial\Omega$, $\Delta u_0=0$ in $\Omega$, and the singular set is $$S_{u_0}=\left\{ z\in\partial\Omega \mbox{ : }u_0 \mbox{ jumps at }z \right\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Logarithmically rescaled boundary-penalized Dirichlet energies Gamma-converge to a counting measure of the jump set.
conclusions: the rescalings $E_\e[u]/\abs{\log\e}$ Gamma-converge when $\e\to 0$ to $\frac{2}{\pi}\mathcal H^0(S_{u_0})$
the minimizers $u_\e$ converge to $u_0$, where $u_0=0,1$ on $\partial\Omega$, $\Delta u_0=0$ in $\Omega$

nodes.name: Conjectured extension to any fractional power $(-\Delta)^\alpha$
nodes.statement: We expect (even if we have no proof) Theorem \ref{th::1} to be true for any power of the Laplacian $(-\Delta)^\alpha$, $\alpha\in(0,1)$, once the layer solutions of \eqref{eq::0} are found.
nodes.statement_short: The convergence result should hold for every fractional power $\alpha\in(0,1)$ once layer solutions exist.
assumptions: once the layer solutions of \eqref{eq::0} are found
conclusions: Theorem \ref{th::1} to be true for any power of the Laplacian $(-\Delta)^\alpha$, $\alpha\in(0,1)$

nodes.name: Cauchy problem (1.5) with $\varepsilon=1$
nodes.statement: \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \displaystyle{v_t=Lv-W'(v) + \sigma(t,x) \quad \mbox{on}\quad (0,T)\times \R}\\ v(0,x)=v_0(x) \quad \mbox{for}\quad x\in\R. \end{array}\right.
nodes.statement_short: The reference Cauchy problem on $(0,T)\times\R$ used to define viscosity solutions.

nodes.name: Definition 2.1 (Viscosity sub and supersolutions)
nodes.statement: {\bf (Viscosity sub and supersolutions)}\\ An upper (respectively lower) semicontinuous function $v\in L^\infty([0,T)\times \R)$ is said to be a subsolution (resp. a supersolution) of (\ref{eq::1ter}) if and only if $$v(0,\cdot)\le v_0^* \quad \mbox{on}\quad \R$$ $$\left(\mbox{resp.}\quad v(0,\cdot)\ge v_0^* \quad \mbox{on}\quad \R\right)$$ and for any $C^2$ test function $\varphi$ satisfying $$v= \varphi \quad \mbox{at the point}\quad (t_0,x_0)\in (0,T)\times \R$$ and $$ v\le \varphi \quad \mbox{on a neighborhood of}\quad \left\{t_0\right\}\times \R$$ $$\left(\mbox{resp.}\quad v\ge \varphi \quad \mbox{on a neighborhood of}\quad \left\{t_0\right\}\times \R\right)$$ then we have $$\varphi_t(t_0,x_0) \le L^1[\varphi(t_0,\cdot),v(t_0,\cdot)](x_0) -W'(\varphi(t_0,x_0)) + \sigma(t_0,x_0)$$ $$\left(\mbox{resp.}\quad \varphi_t(t_0,x_0) \ge L^1[\varphi(t_0,\cdot),v(t_0,\cdot)](x_0) -W'(\varphi(t_0,x_0)) + \sigma(t_0,x_0) \right)$$ where for any functions $\Phi(x), w(x)$ we set $$L^1[\Phi,w](x_0)=\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{[-1,1]}\frac{dz}{z^2}\left(\Phi(x_0+z)-\Phi(x_0)-z\Phi'(x_0) \right) + \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{\R\backslash [-1,1]}\frac{dz}{z^2}\left(w(x_0+z)-w(x_0)\right).$$ A function $v\in L^\infty([0,T)\times \R)$ is said to be a viscosity solution of (\ref{eq::1ter}), if and only if $v^*$ is a subsolution and $v_*$ is a supersolution.\\ Finally, a function $v\in L^\infty_{loc}([0,+\infty )\times \R)$ is said to be a viscosity solution on $[0,+\infty)\times \R$, if and only if its is a viscosity solution on $[0,T)\times \R$ for any $T>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Semicontinuous $v$ is a sub/supersolution when the split operator $L^1[\varphi,v]$ inequality holds against $C^2$ test functions touching $v$.
differentia: for any $C^2$ test function $\varphi$ satisfying $v= \varphi$ at the point $(t_0,x_0)$ and $v\le \varphi$ on a neighborhood of $\left\{t_0\right\}\times \R$ then $\varphi_t(t_0,x_0) \le L^1[\varphi(t_0,\cdot),v(t_0,\cdot)](x_0) -W'(\varphi(t_0,x_0)) + \sigma(t_0,x_0)$

nodes.name: Remark 2.2 (Classical solutions are viscosity solutions)
nodes.statement: {\bf (Classical solutions are viscosity solutions)}\\ From this definition, we can easily check that every function $v\in L^\infty([0,T)\times \R)\cap C^{1,\beta}_{loc}([0,T)\times \R)$ for some $0<\beta<1$, is indeed a viscosity solution if and only if it is a classical solution of (\ref{eq::1ter}). This is mainly due to the fact that $v_t$ and $Lv(t,\cdot)$ are then defined pointwise.

nodes.name: Proposition 2.3 (Perron's method)
nodes.statement: {\bf (Perron's method)}\\ Assume that there exists a supersolution $\underline{v}$ and a subsolution $\overline{v}$ of equation (\ref{eq::1ter}) satisfying $$\underline{v} \le \overline{v} \quad \mbox{on}\quad [0,T)\times \R.$$ Then there exists a viscosity solution $v$ of (\ref{eq::1ter}) satisfying $$\underline{v} \le v\le \overline{v} \quad \mbox{on}\quad [0,T)\times \R.$$
assumptions: Assume that there exists a supersolution $\underline{v}$ and a subsolution $\overline{v}$ of equation (\ref{eq::1ter}) satisfying $\underline{v} \le \overline{v}$ on $[0,T)\times \R$
conclusions: there exists a viscosity solution $v$ of (\ref{eq::1ter}) satisfying $\underline{v} \le v\le \overline{v}$ on $[0,T)\times \R$

nodes.name: Proposition 2.4 (Comparison principle)
nodes.statement: {\bf (Comparison principle)}\\ Assume that $\underline{v}$ is a subsolution (resp. $\overline{v}$ is a supersolution) of equation (\ref{eq::1ter}) on $[0,T)$ such that $$\underline{v}(0,x)\le \overline{v}(0,x)\quad \mbox{for all}\quad x\in \R.$$ Then $$\underline{v}\le \overline{v}\quad \mbox{on}\quad [0,T)\times \R.$$
assumptions: $\underline{v}$ is a subsolution (resp. $\overline{v}$ is a supersolution) of equation (\ref{eq::1ter}) on $[0,T)$

nodes.name: Rewritten rescaled equation used for the formal ansatz
nodes.statement: \displaystyle{-\varepsilon v^\varepsilon_t=\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\left\{W'(v^\varepsilon) -\varepsilon Lv^\varepsilon - \varepsilon \sigma \right\}\quad \mbox{on}\quad (0,+\infty)\times \R.}

nodes.name: Transition-layer equation $L\phi-W'(\phi)=0$
nodes.statement: L\phi-W'(\phi)=0.

nodes.name: First-order matching condition $W''(0)\tilde{\sigma}=\sigma$
nodes.statement: W''(0) \tilde{\sigma} =\sigma.

nodes.name: Corrector equation obtained from the second ansatz
nodes.statement: L\psi - W''(\phi)\psi = \frac{\dot{x}_1}{c} \phi' - \frac{\tilde{\sigma}}{c}(W''(\phi)-W''(0)).
nodes.statement_short: Linearized equation the corrector $\psi$ must satisfy at order $\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Theorem 3.1 (Existence and properties of the layer solution)
nodes.statement: {\bf (Existence and properties of the layer solution)}\\ Under assumption Ai), there exists a unique solution $\phi$ of (\ref{eq::0bis}). Moreover $\phi \in C^{1,\beta}_{loc}(\R)$ for some $0<\beta <1$, and there exists a constant $C>0$ such that \begin{equation} 0<\phi'(x)\le \frac{C}{1+x^2} \quad \mbox{for all}\quad x\in\R \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \left|\phi(x)-H(x)+\frac{1}{\alpha \pi x}\right| \quad \le \quad \frac{C}{x^2} \quad \mbox{for all}\quad |x|\ge 1 \end{equation} where $H$ is the Heaviside function and $\alpha=W''(0)$.
nodes.section: 3.2 The layer solution and the corrector
nodes.statement_short: The layer profile $\phi$ exists, is unique and $C^{1,\beta}_{loc}$, with sharp $1/x$ decay towards the Heaviside function.
conclusions: there exists a unique solution $\phi$ of (\ref{eq::0bis})

nodes.name: Corrector problem for $\psi$
nodes.statement: \left\{\begin{array}{l} L\psi -W''(\phi)\psi=\phi'+ \eta (W''(\phi)-W''(0)) \quad \mbox{on}\quad \R,\\ \psi(-\infty)=0 = \psi(+\infty) \end{array}\right.
nodes.section: 3.2 The layer solution and the corrector
nodes.statement_short: Linear nonlocal equation for the corrector $\psi$ with vanishing limits at $\pm\infty$.

nodes.name: Normalization constant $\eta$
nodes.section: 3.2 The layer solution and the corrector

nodes.name: Theorem 3.2 (Existence and properties of the corrector)
nodes.statement: {\bf (Existence and properties of the corrector)}\\ Under assumption Ai), there exists a unique solution $\psi \in H^{\frac12}(\R)$ of (\ref{eq::7}). Moreover $\psi \in C^{1,\beta}_{loc}(\R)\cap L^\infty (\R)$ for some $0<\beta< 1$ and $$|\psi'|_{L^\infty(\R)} < +\infty. $$
nodes.section: 3.2 The layer solution and the corrector
nodes.statement_short: The corrector $\psi$ exists, is unique in $H^{1/2}$, and is bounded with bounded derivative.
conclusions: there exists a unique solution $\psi \in H^{\frac12}(\R)$ of (\ref{eq::7})

nodes.name: Lemma 3.3 (Lower bound on the distance between particles)
nodes.statement: {\bf (Lower bound on the distance between particles, \cite{Forcadel-Imbert-Monneau:homogeneization})}\\ Let $(x_i(t))_{i=1,...,N}$ be the solution of (\ref{eq::2bis}) on $[0,T]$ and let $$d(t):=\min\{\abs{x_i(t)-x_j(t)},i\neq j\}$$ be the minimal distance between particles. Then under assumptions Ai) and Aii), we have for all $t\in [0,T]$ $$d(t)\ge d(0) e^{-Ct} \quad \mbox{with}\quad C=\gamma K$$ where $K$ is the space Lipschitz constant of $\sigma$.
nodes.statement_short: The minimal inter-particle distance decays at worst exponentially, so particles never collide in finite time.
assumptions: Let $(x_i(t))_{i=1,...,N}$ be the solution of (\ref{eq::2bis}) on $[0,T]$
conclusions: for all $t\in [0,T]$ $d(t)\ge d(0) e^{-Ct}$ with $C=\gamma K$

nodes.name: Corollary 3.4 (Long time existence of a solution to the ODE system)
nodes.statement: {\bf (Long time existence of a solution to the ODE system)}\\ Under assumption (A), there exists a unique solution $(x_i(t))_{i=1,...,N}$ of (\ref{eq::2bis}) on $[0,+\infty)$.
conclusions: there exists a unique solution $(x_i(t))_{i=1,...,N}$ of (\ref{eq::2bis}) on $[0,+\infty)$

nodes.name: Supersolution ansatz $\overline{v}^\varepsilon$ and shifted particles $\overline{x}_i$
nodes.statement: We want to build a supersolution with a parameter $\delta>0$ to fix later. We define $(\overline{x}_i(t))_{i=1,...,N}$ as the solution of $$\left\{\begin{array}{l} \displaystyle{\frac{d\overline{x}_i}{dt}= \gamma \left(-\delta-\sigma(\overline{x}_i,t) + \frac{1}{\pi}\sum_{j\not= i} \frac{1}{\overline{x}_i-\overline{x}_j}\right),\quad \mbox{on}\quad (0,+\infty)},\\ \overline{x}_i(0)=x_i^0-\delta, \end{array}\right| \quad \mbox{for}\quad i=1,...,N$$ with $\gamma$ given in (\ref{eq::2'}).\\ We also define $$\overline{v}^\varepsilon(t,x)=\varepsilon \tilde{\sigma}(t,x) + \sum_{i=1}^N \left\{\phi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_i(t)}{\varepsilon}\right) -\varepsilon\overline{c}_i(t)\psi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_i(t)}{\varepsilon}\right) \right\}$$ where $$\left\{\begin{array}{l} \overline{c}_i(t) = \dot{\overline{x}}_i(t)\\ \\ \displaystyle{\tilde{\sigma}=\frac{\delta+\sigma}{\alpha} \quad \mbox{with}\quad \alpha=W''(0)>0} \end{array}\right.$$ and $\phi$ is given in Theorem \ref{th::5} and $\psi$ in Theorem \ref{th::6}.
nodes.section: 4 The convergence result: proof of Theorem 1.1
nodes.statement_short: Candidate supersolution built from $\delta$-shifted particle trajectories plus layer and corrector profiles.

nodes.name: Proposition 4.1 (Supersolution at the initial time)
nodes.statement: {\bf (Supersolution at the initial time)}\\ Under assumption (A), there exists $\delta_0>0$ such that for all $0<\delta\le \delta_0$, we have \begin{equation} \overline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x)\ge v_0^\varepsilon(x) \quad \mbox{for all}\quad x\in\R \end{equation} for $\varepsilon >0$ small enough.
nodes.section: 4 The convergence result: proof of Theorem 1.1
conclusions: there exists $\delta_0>0$ such that $\overline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x)\ge v_0^\varepsilon(x)$ for all $x\in\R$

nodes.name: Proposition 4.3 (Supersolution for positive time)
nodes.statement: {\bf (Supersolution for positive time)}\\ Under assumption (A), there exists $\delta_0>0$ such that for all $0<\delta\le \delta_0$ and given $T>0$, we have \begin{equation} \overline{v}^\varepsilon_t \ge \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \left(L\overline{v}^\varepsilon - \frac{1}{\varepsilon} W'(\overline{v}^\varepsilon) +\sigma(t,x) \right) \quad \mbox{on}\quad (0,T)\times \R \end{equation} for $\varepsilon >0$ small enough.
nodes.section: 4 The convergence result: proof of Theorem 1.1
conclusions: there exists $\delta_0>0$ such that $\overline{v}^\varepsilon_t \ge \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \left(L\overline{v}^\varepsilon - \frac{1}{\varepsilon} W'(\overline{v}^\varepsilon) +\sigma(t,x) \right)$ on $(0,T)\times \R$

nodes.name: Fourier transform on the Schwartz space
nodes.statement: We recall our definition of the Fourier transform for $w \in {\mathcal S}(\R)$ (where ${\mathcal S}(\R)$ is the Schwartz space): $$\widehat{w}(\xi)=\int_{\R}w(x) \ e^{-i\xi x}dx \quad \mbox{for all}\quad \xi\in\R$$

nodes.name: The Hilbert space $H^{1/2}(\R)$
nodes.statement: and recall the definition of the following Hilbert space $$H^{\frac12}(\R)=\left\{w\in L^2(\R),\quad \int_{\R}d\xi\ (1+|\xi|)|\widehat{w}(\xi)|^2 < +\infty \right\}$$ with the scalar product $$(v,w)_{H^{\frac12}(\R)}=\int_{\R}d\xi\ (1+|\xi|)\widehat{v}^*(\xi) \widehat{w}(\xi)$$ where $\widehat{v}^*$ denotes here the complex conjugate of $\widehat{v}$.

nodes.name: The Hilbert space $H^{-1/2}(\R)$
nodes.statement: We also set the following Hilbert space $$H^{-\frac12}(\R)=\left\{w\in {\mathcal S}'(\R),\quad \widehat{w}\in L^2_{loc}(\R),\quad \int_{\R}d\xi\ (1+|\xi|)^{-1}|\widehat{w}(\xi)|^2 < +\infty \right\}$$ with the scalar product $$(v,w)_{H^{-\frac12}(\R)}=\int_{\R}d\xi\ (1+|\xi|)^{-1}\widehat{v}^*(\xi) \widehat{w}(\xi).$$ It is known that $H^{-\frac12}(\R)$ is the dual of $H^{\frac12}(\R)$.

nodes.name: Fourier definition of the half-Laplacian
nodes.statement: \widehat{Lw}(\xi):=-|\xi|\widehat{w}(\xi) \quad \mbox{for}\quad \xi\in\R.

nodes.name: Continuity and self-adjointness of $L$ on $H^{1/2}$
nodes.statement: In particular, $L$ is a continuous linear mapping from $H^{\frac12}(\R)$ into $H^{-\frac12}(\R)$ satisfying $$\norm{Lw}_{H^{-\frac12}(\R)}\le \norm{w}_{H^{\frac12}(\R)}.$$ Moreover $L$ is self-adjoint as follows: for any $v,w \in H^{\frac12}(\R)$, we have $$<Lv,w>_{H^{-\frac12}(\R)\times H^{\frac12}(\R)}= <Lw,v>_{H^{-\frac12}(\R)\times H^{\frac12}(\R)}.$$
nodes.statement_short: $L:H^{1/2}\to H^{-1/2}$ is a norm-nonincreasing continuous linear map and is self-adjoint for the duality pairing.
conclusions: $L$ is a continuous linear mapping from $H^{\frac12}(\R)$ into $H^{-\frac12}(\R)$ satisfying $\norm{Lw}_{H^{-\frac12}(\R)}\le \norm{w}_{H^{\frac12}(\R)}$

nodes.name: Theorem 5.1 (The L\'evy-Khintchine formula)
nodes.statement: {\bf (The L\'evy-Khintchine formula)}\\ For any $0<\beta<1$, if $w\in H^{\frac12}(\R)\cap C^{1,\beta}_{loc}(\R)$, then we have $$Lw(x)=\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{\R}\frac{dz}{z^2}\left(w(x+z)-w(x)-zw'(x) 1_{\left\{|z|\le 1\right\}}\right).$$ Moreover this formula allows also to define $Lw$ for instance for $w\in L^\infty(\R)\cap C^{1,\beta}_{loc}(\R)$.
conclusions: this formula allows also to define $Lw$ for instance for $w\in L^\infty(\R)\cap C^{1,\beta}_{loc}(\R)$

nodes.name: Remark 5.2 (truncation radius is immaterial)
nodes.statement: In the previous formula the characteristic function $1_{\left\{|z|\le 1\right\}}$ can be replaced by $1_{\left\{|z|\le r\right\}}$ for any $r>0$, which does not change the value of the integral.

nodes.name: Gagliardo-seminorm identity for the half-Laplacian
nodes.statement: \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\R}d\xi\ |\xi||\widehat{w}(\xi)|^2=<-Lw,w>_{H^{-\frac12}(\R)\times H^{\frac12}(\R)} = {\frac{1}{2\pi}} \int_{\R\times \R} dx dx' \ \frac{|w(x')-w(x)|^2}{|x'-x|^2}.

nodes.name: Harmonic extension problem on the upper half-plane
nodes.statement: \left\{\begin{array}{ll} \Delta u = 0 &\quad \mbox{on}\quad \Omega,\\ \\ u(x,0)=w(x) &\quad \mbox{for all}\quad x\in\partial\Omega. \end{array}\right.
nodes.section: 5.2.1 Classical harmonic extension for smooth functions with compact support

nodes.name: Dirichlet-to-Neumann identity for the half-Laplacian
nodes.statement: Lw(x)=-\frac{\partial u}{\partial \nu}(x,0) \quad \mbox{for all}\quad x\in\partial\Omega.

nodes.name: Definition 5.5 (Weak sub/super/solution)
nodes.statement: {\bf (Weak sub/super/solution)}\\ Let $d$ be a measurable bounded function on $\mathbb R$, and let $g\in L^2(\mathbb R)$. We say that $w\in H^\half(\mathbb R)$ is a weak supersolution for the equation \begin{equation} Lw -d(x)w=g \quad \mbox{ on }\partial\Omega \end{equation} if, for $u:=P*_x w$ and $$B(u,v):=\int_{\Omega}\nabla u\cdot\nabla v+\int_{\partial\Omega} d(x)(Tu)(Tv),$$ we have that \beB(u,v)\geq \int_{\partial\Omega} gTv\quad\mbox{for all }v\in H.\ee Respectively, $w$ is a weak subsolution if \be B(u,v)\leq \int_{\partial\Omega} gTv\quad\mbox{for all }v\in H.\ee Accordingly, we say that $w$ is a weak solution if it is both a weak sub and supersolution.
nodes.statement_short: Weak sub/supersolutions of $Lw-d(x)w=g$ defined by one-sided inequalities for the bilinear form $B$ against all $v\in H$.
nodes.definiendum: weak supersolution / weak subsolution / weak solution

nodes.name: Lemma 5.6 (Equivalence of solutions)
nodes.statement: {\bf (Equivalence of solutions)}\\ Given $w\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb R)\cap \mathcal C^{1,\beta}_{\mbox{loc}}(\mathbb R)$, the following two ways of compuing $Lw$, i.e, \begin{enumerate} \item as a Dirichlet to Neumann operator (see section 5.3.1., in particular \eqref{eq::4}-\eqref{eq::55}); \item using the L\'evy-Khintchine formula (see theorem \ref{th::2}), \end{enumerate} are equivalent. If, in addition, $w\in H^\half(\mathbb R)$, then the half-Laplacian definition in term of distributions as given in theorem \ref{th::4} is also equivalent. As a consequence, the notions of viscosity and weak solutions from Definitions \ref{defi::1} and \ref{defi-weak-solution}, respectively, coincide in the smooth case.
nodes.statement_short: Dirichlet-to-Neumann, L\'evy-Khintchine and distributional definitions of $L$ agree, so viscosity and weak solutions coincide for smooth functions.
conclusions: the following two ways of compuing $Lw$ ... are equivalent

nodes.name: Theorem 5.7 ($L^p$ bound for the Poisson integral)

nodes.name: Theorem 5.10 (Known existence and properties of the layer solution)
nodes.statement: {\bf (Known existence and properties of the layer solution)}\\ Let $f$ be any $\mathcal C^{1,\beta}$ function with $0 < \beta < 1$ and such that $W'= -f$. Then there exists a layer solution $u_W\in \mathcal C^{2,\beta}_{\mbox{loc}}(\overline\Omega)$ of \eqref{Cabre-SolaMorales-layer} if and only if $$W'(0)=W'(1)=0\quad\mbox{and}\quad W> W(0)=W(1)\quad\mbox{in } (0,1).$$ Moreover, \begin{enumerate} \item If $W''(0), W''(1)>0$, then a layer solution of \eqref{Cabre-SolaMorales-layer} is unique up to translations in the $x$ variable, and it satisfies \be(u_W)_x>0\quad\mbox{in }\overline{\Omega}.\ee \item We have the estimate \be\abs{\nabla u_W(x,y)}\leq \frac{C}{1+\abs{(x,y)}}, \quad \mbox{for all }x\in\mathbb R, y\geq 0.\ee \item Set $\phi(x):=u_W(x,0)$. We have the bounds \begin{equation} \abs{\phi(x)-H(x)}\leq \frac{C}{1+\abs{x}} \quad\mbox{for all }x\in\mathbb R, \end{equation} \be \frac{C_1}{1+\abs{x}^2} \leq \phi'(x)\leq \frac{C_2}{1+\abs{x}^2},\quad \mbox{for all }x\in\mathbb R, \ee for some positive constants $C,C_1,C_2$. \item A layer solution is always a stable solution. This means that \be\int_{\Omega}\abs{\nabla v}^2+\int_{\partial\Omega}W''(\phi)v^2\geq 0\ee for every function $v\in\mathcal C^1(\overline{\Omega})$ with compact support in $\overline{\Omega}$.\\ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Layer solutions exist iff the potential is a balanced double well; they are unique up to translation, monotone, gradient-decaying and stable.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.1
nodes.statement: First we choose $\delta>0$ small enough such that $$x^0_i<\overline{x}_{i+1}(0)< x_{i+1}^0 \quad \mbox{for}\quad i=1,...,N-1.$$ Let $A>0$ be large enough such that \begin{equation} \frac{\delta}{\alpha} \ge \left(\sum_{i=1}^N |\overline{c}_i(0)|\right)\ \sup_{\R\backslash [-A,A]} |\psi|. \end{equation} \noindent {\bf Case 1: $|x-\overline{x}_i(0)|\ge \varepsilon A$ for each $i=1,...,N$}\\ Using the fact that $\phi$ is increasing, we deduce that $\displaystyle{\phi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_i(0)}{\varepsilon}\right) \ge \phi\left(\frac{x-{x}_i^0}{\varepsilon}\right)}$ and then using (\ref{eq::10}), we get that $$\overline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x)\ge v_0^\varepsilon(x).$$ \noindent {\bf Case 2: $|x-\overline{x}_{i_0}(0)| < \varepsilon A$ for some index $i_0\in \left\{1,...,N\right\}$}\\ Then $$\phi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_{i_0}(0)}{\varepsilon}\right)\ge \phi(-A)>0$$ while $$\begin{array}{ll} \displaystyle{\phi\left(\frac{x-{x}_{i_0}^0}{\varepsilon}\right)} & = \displaystyle{\phi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_{i_0}(0)-\delta}{\varepsilon}\right)}\\ \\ & \displaystyle{\le \phi\left(A-\frac{\delta}{\varepsilon}\right) = O\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{\delta}\right) \quad \mbox{as}\quad \varepsilon \to 0.} \end{array}$$ Therefore for $\varepsilon$ small enough, we have $$\displaystyle{\phi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_{i_0}(0)}{\varepsilon}\right) \ge \phi\left(\frac{x-{x}_{i_0}^0}{\varepsilon}\right) +\sum_{i=1}^N \varepsilon \overline{c}_i(0) \psi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_{i}(0)}{\varepsilon}\right)}.$$ Using again the monotonicity of $\phi$, we conclude in case 2 that $$\overline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x)\ge v_0^\varepsilon(x).$$ Finally case 1 and 2 prove that (\ref{eq::8}) holds for any $x\in\R$. This ends the proof of the Proposition.

nodes.statement_short: Integrate $\bar u$ in $y$ and use elliptic $W^{2,2}$ estimates in the strip $0<y<R$.

nodes.name: Step 2: finiteness of the Dirichlet energy far from the boundary
nodes.statement:
oindent \emph{Step 2: $\int_{\left\{y>Right\}}|
abla  ar u|^2 < +\infty$.}\ Far away from the boundary of $\Omega$, we can use standard interior gradient estimates (Lemma ef{local-grad-estimates}) for the harmonic function $ ar u$, say, at a ball $B_{1}(x,y)\subset \Omega$ so that $$\abs{
abla  ar u(x,y)}\leq C 
orm{ ar u}_{L^\infty (B_{1}(x,y))}\le  rac{C'}{1+(|(x,y)|-1)^2}$$ where we have used (ef{gradient-bound}) in the last inequality.
nodes.statement_short: Interior gradient estimates for harmonic functions give quadratic decay.

nodes.name: Step 3: Conclusion that $\bar u\in H$
nodes.statement: \noindent \emph{Step 3: Conclusion.}\\ From Steps 1 and 2, we get that $\bar u\in H$.
nodes.statement_short: Steps 1 and 2 together give $\bar u\in H$.

nodes.name: Step 4: $\phi'$ solves the linearized equation weakly
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate the weak formulation in $x$ and conclude $B(\bar u,v)=0$ by density.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 5.13
nodes.statement:
Fix $a:=2/	au$, and consider the model layer solution $u^a$ given in \eqref{model-layer}, with trace $\phi^a$. Because of hypothesis on $M$ and the decay of $(\phi^a)_x$ from \eqref{derivative-bound}, we can find a positive constant $K$ such that $\abs{M(x)}\leq K \phi^{a}_x(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb R$. Next, compute $$ rac{\partial v}{\partial 
u}+d(x) v=M(x)\leq K u^{a}_x\leq K\left[ rac{2}{	au} rac{\partial u_x^{a}}{\partial
u}+2u_x^{a}ight]\leq  rac{2K}{	au} \left[ rac{\partial u_x^{a}}{\partial
u}+d(x) u_x^{a}ight]\quad\mbox{along }\partial\Omega,$$ where we have used \eqref{computation-layer} in the second inequality. Now we apply Lemma ef{lema-comparison} to the difference $\left[ rac{2K}{	au}u_x^{a}-vight]$ to get $v\le  rac{2K}{	au}u_x^{a}$ in $ ar\Omega$. The same argument, applied to $-v$ gives that $\abs{v}\le  rac{2K}{	au}u_x^{a}$. Taking into account the estimate \eqref{derivative-bound}, we achieve the conclusion of the corollary.
nodes.section: 5.5 Comparison principles for smooth enough solutions
nodes.statement_short: Compare $v$ with a multiple of the explicit barrier $u^a_x$ via the strong comparison principle.

nodes.name: Build the explicit barrier $u^a_x$
nodes.statement: Fix $a:=2/\tau$, and consider the model layer solution $u^a$ given in \eqref{model-layer}, with trace $\phi^a$. Because of hypothesis on $M$ and the decay of $(\phi^a)_x$ from \eqref{derivative-bound}, we can find a positive constant $K$ such that $\abs{M(x)}\leq K \phi^{a}_x(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb R$.
nodes.section: 5.5 Comparison principles for smooth enough solutions
nodes.statement_short: Choose $a=2/\tau$ and dominate $M$ by a multiple of $\phi^a_x$.

nodes.name: Chain of inequalities along the boundary
nodes.statement:
Next, compute $$ rac{\partial v}{\partial 
u}+d(x) v=M(x)\leq K u^{a}_x\leq K\left[ rac{2}{	au} rac{\partial u_x^{a}}{\partial
u}+2u_x^{a}ight]\leq  rac{2K}{	au} \left[ rac{\partial u_x^{a}}{\partial
u}+d(x) u_x^{a}ight]\quad\mbox{along }\partial\Omega,$$ where we have used \eqref{computation-layer} in the second inequality.
nodes.section: 5.5 Comparison principles for smooth enough solutions
nodes.statement_short: Convert the bound on $M$ into a Robin differential inequality for the barrier.

nodes.name: Apply the strong comparison principle and conclude
nodes.statement: Now we apply Lemma \ref{lema-comparison} to the difference $\left[\frac{2K}{\tau}u_x^{a}-v\right]$ to get $v\le \frac{2K}{\tau}u_x^{a}$ in $\bar\Omega$. The same argument, applied to $-v$ gives that $\abs{v}\le \frac{2K}{\tau}u_x^{a}$. Taking into account the estimate \eqref{derivative-bound}, we achieve the conclusion of the corollary.
nodes.section: 5.5 Comparison principles for smooth enough solutions
nodes.statement_short: Comparison applied to $\pm v$ gives $|v|\le (2K/\tau)u^a_x$, hence the decay.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.14
nodes.statement: This is a small variation of the classical proof for the Laplacian, that can be found in Gilbarg-Trudinger \cite{Gilbarg-Trudinger}, Theorem 8.1. Note that $(Tu)^-= T(u^-)$ a.e. in $\mathbb R$. Set $$\Omega^-:=supp (u^-)\quad\mbox{and}\quad\Theta:=supp((Tu)^-)\subset \mathbb R.$$ We know that $\Omega^-$ is contained in $\mathbb R^2_+\backslash B_R^+$ and $\Theta\subset \mathbb R\backslash(-R,R)$. Use $u^-\in H$ as an admissible test function in \eqref{weak-super-solution}; then $$0\leq -\int_{\Omega^-} \abs{\nabla u}^2-\int_{\Theta}d(x)u^2.$$ The proof is easily completed.
nodes.statement_short: Test the weak supersolution inequality with the negative part $u^-$.

nodes.name: Reduce to the classical Laplacian argument
nodes.statement: This is a small variation of the classical proof for the Laplacian, that can be found in Gilbarg-Trudinger \cite{Gilbarg-Trudinger}, Theorem 8.1. Note that $(Tu)^-= T(u^-)$ a.e. in $\mathbb R$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the classical proof scheme and that $(Tu)^-=T(u^-)$.

nodes.name: Localize the supports of the negative parts
nodes.statement: Set $$\Omega^-:=supp (u^-)\quad\mbox{and}\quad\Theta:=supp((Tu)^-)\subset \mathbb R.$$ We know that $\Omega^-$ is contained in $\mathbb R^2_+\backslash B_R^+$ and $\Theta\subset \mathbb R\backslash(-R,R)$.
nodes.statement_short: The supports $\Omega^-$ and $\Theta$ avoid the half-ball $B_R^+$.

nodes.name: Test with $u^-$ and conclude
nodes.statement: Use $u^-\in H$ as an admissible test function in \eqref{weak-super-solution}; then $$0\leq -\int_{\Omega^-} \abs{\nabla u}^2-\int_{\Theta}d(x)u^2.$$ The proof is easily completed.
nodes.statement_short: Using $u^-$ as test function forces both non-negative terms to vanish.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.15
nodes.statement_short: Moser iteration: test with powers of $u^+$, upgrade integrability by the trace and Sobolev inequalities, then iterate.

nodes.name: Insert the power test function $v=(u^+)^\sigma$
nodes.statement: This is the classical proof by Moser for the Laplacian case. We follow closely the arguments from Theorems 8.15 and 8.18 in Gilbarg-Trudinger \cite{Gilbarg-Trudinger}, so we will not give every single detail here. Assume that $w$ is a subsolution, and set $u:=P*_x w$. Given $\sigma\ge 1$, we insert into \eqref{weak-sub-solution}, the test function $$v=(u^+)^\sigma.$$ Note that $Tv=(Tu)^\sigma$ a.e.. Here we point out that this $v$ might not belong to $H$; in order to make the argument rigorous, a truncated version must be used instead in the definition of $v$, say replacing $u^+$ by \begin{equation} \min\{u^+,n\},\quad \mbox{for}\quad n\in \mathbb N. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Use (a truncation of) $(u^+)^\sigma$ as test function in the weak subsolution inequality.

nodes.name: Derive the energy inequality for $u_1=(u^+)^\gamma$
nodes.statement_short: Obtain $\int|\nabla u_1|^2\le C_1(\gamma)\int w_1^2$ with an explicit constant.

nodes.name: Upgrade integrability via trace and Sobolev inequalities
nodes.statement: For the left hand side, we proceed as follows. We use the trace inequality \eqref{trace-inequality} to estimate $$\frac{1}{2\pi}\norm{w_1}^2_{\dot H^{\half}(\mathbb R)} \le \int_{\Omega} \abs{\nabla u_1}^2.$$ But, on the other hand, by Theorem \ref{Sobolev}, for every $p>1$, there exists a constant $C_p>0$ such that $$\begin{array}{ll} ||w_1||^2_{L^{2p}}&\le C_p\left(||w_1||^2_{L^2}+||w_1||^2_{\dot{H}^{\frac12}}\right)\\ \\ &\le C_2(\gamma) ||w_1||^2_{L^2} \quad \mbox{with}\quad C_2(\gamma)=C_p(1+2\pi C_1(\gamma)), \end{array}$$ where we have used \eqref{moser-1} in the last line.\\ If we denote $$\Psi (q):=\lp\int_{\partial\Omega} \abs{w^+}^{q}\rp^{\frac{1}{q}},$$ then we have shown that $$\Psi(2p\gamma)\leq \left[C_2(\gamma)\right]^{\frac{1}{2\gamma}}\Psi(2\gamma).$$
nodes.statement_short: Combine the trace inequality with the Sobolev embedding to get $\Psi(2p\gamma)\le C_2(\gamma)^{1/2\gamma}\Psi(2\gamma)$.

nodes.name: Iterate over $\gamma_m=p^m$
nodes.statement: Fixed $p>1$ and choose $\gamma_m=p^m$ for $m\in\N$; by iteration we know \be\Psi(2\gamma_m)\leq C_m\Psi(2),\quad \forall m\in\mathbb N\backslash\left\{0\right\},\quad C_m:=\prod_{j=0}^{m-1} \left[C_2(\gamma_j)\right]^\frac{1}{2\gamma_j}.\ee It is then easy to check that $C_m\le C_\infty$ uniformly bounded in $m\in\mathbb N$ (which is also shown, for instance, in page 190 of \cite{Gilbarg-Trudinger}).
nodes.statement_short: Iterate the reverse-Hölder step with uniformly bounded product constants.

nodes.name: Pass to the limit and conclude the $L^\infty$ bound
nodes.statement: Remark that $$\sup_{(-R,R)} \abs{w^+}=\lim_{q\to\infty} \lp\frac{1}{2R} \int_{(-R,R)} \abs{w^+}^q\rp^{\frac{1}{q}}.$$ Letting $m$ to infinity in \eqref{iteration-step}, we have $$\sup_{(-R,R)} \abs{w^+}\leq C_\infty \norm{w^+}_{L^{2}(\mathbb R)},$$ for every $R>0$. We get the first part of the conclusion, taking $R\to +\infty$ and then $n\to +\infty$ in (\ref{eq::902}). The second part is analogous, using $u^-$ instead. The final assertion is an immediate consequence of Theorem \ref{thm-Stein}.
nodes.statement_short: Let $m,R,n\to\infty$ to get $\sup w\le C\|w^+\|_{L^2}$; the supersolution case is symmetric.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 5.16
nodes.statement: We use Proposition \ref{prop-moser-iteration} with some modifications in order to account for the extra right hand side term involving $g$. By hypothesis, $w$ is a weak solution satisfying for all $v\in H$, $$B(u,v)=-\int_{\partial\Omega} gv, \quad\mbox{for }u=P*_x w.$$ Similarly as before (using if necessary a truncated version), we use the test function $v=\abs{u}^{\sigma-1} u$, $u_1=|u|^{\gamma-1}u$ and $w_1 = Tu_1$. We use H\"older inequality with exponents $2\gamma$, $\frac{2\gamma}{2\gamma-1}$, which gives $$\abs{\int_{\partial\Omega} gv}\leq \lp\int_{\partial\Omega} \abs{g}^{2\gamma}\rp^{\frac{1}{2\gamma}} \lp\int_{\partial\Omega} w_1^{2}\rp^{\frac{2\gamma-1}{2\gamma}},$$ we get \begin{equation*}\begin{split} \int_{\Omega} \abs{\nabla u_1}^2 &\le C_1(\gamma) \int_{\partial\Omega} w_1^{2} +\tilde{C}_1(\gamma)\lp\int_{\partial\Omega} w_1^{2}\rp^{\frac{2\gamma-1}{2\gamma}}\quad \mbox{with}\quad \tilde{C}_1(\gamma)= \frac{\gamma^2}{2\gamma-1}\cdot \left(\int_{\partial \Omega} |g|^{2\gamma}\right)^{\frac{1}{2\gamma}}. \end{split}\end{equation*} Assuming (\ref{eq::904}) with $2\gamma\ge p_0$, we get $$\int_{\Omega} \abs{\nabla u_1}^2 \le \bar{C}_1(\gamma) \max\left\{1,\int_{\partial \Omega} w_1^2\right\} \quad \mbox{with}\quad \bar{C}_1(\gamma) = C_1(\gamma) + \frac{c\gamma^2}{2\gamma-1}$$ The rest of the argument follows similarly, with $\bar{C}_2(\gamma)=\max\left\{1,C_p(1+2\pi \bar{C}_1(\gamma))\right\}$, $\bar\Psi(q)=\max \left\{1,\left(\int_{\partial\Omega}|w|^q\right)^{\frac1q}\right\}$, and $\bar \Psi(2p\gamma)\le (\bar C_2(\gamma))^{\frac{1}{2\gamma}}\bar \Psi(2\gamma)$, starting the iteration at $2\gamma=p_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat the Moser iteration with a H\"older-controlled extra term coming from $g$.

nodes.name: Set up the weak formulation with right-hand side $g$
nodes.statement: We use Proposition \ref{prop-moser-iteration} with some modifications in order to account for the extra right hand side term involving $g$. By hypothesis, $w$ is a weak solution satisfying for all $v\in H$, $$B(u,v)=-\int_{\partial\Omega} gv, \quad\mbox{for }u=P*_x w.$$
nodes.statement_short: Write the weak solution identity $B(u,v)=-\int g v$.

nodes.name: H\"older estimate of the extra term
nodes.statement: Similarly as before (using if necessary a truncated version), we use the test function $v=\abs{u}^{\sigma-1} u$, $u_1=|u|^{\gamma-1}u$ and $w_1 = Tu_1$. We use H\"older inequality with exponents $2\gamma$, $\frac{2\gamma}{2\gamma-1}$, which gives $$\abs{\int_{\partial\Omega} gv}\leq \lp\int_{\partial\Omega} \abs{g}^{2\gamma}\rp^{\frac{1}{2\gamma}} \lp\int_{\partial\Omega} w_1^{2}\rp^{\frac{2\gamma-1}{2\gamma}},$$ we get \begin{equation*}\begin{split} \int_{\Omega} \abs{\nabla u_1}^2 &\le C_1(\gamma) \int_{\partial\Omega} w_1^{2} +\tilde{C}_1(\gamma)\lp\int_{\partial\Omega} w_1^{2}\rp^{\frac{2\gamma-1}{2\gamma}}\quad \mbox{with}\quad \tilde{C}_1(\gamma)= \frac{\gamma^2}{2\gamma-1}\cdot \left(\int_{\partial \Omega} |g|^{2\gamma}\right)^{\frac{1}{2\gamma}}. \end{split}\end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: H\"older with exponents $2\gamma$ and $2\gamma/(2\gamma-1)$ bounds the $g$-contribution.

nodes.name: Use the uniform $L^p$ bound on $g$ and iterate
nodes.statement: Assuming (\ref{eq::904}) with $2\gamma\ge p_0$, we get $$\int_{\Omega} \abs{\nabla u_1}^2 \le \bar{C}_1(\gamma) \max\left\{1,\int_{\partial \Omega} w_1^2\right\} \quad \mbox{with}\quad \bar{C}_1(\gamma) = C_1(\gamma) + \frac{c\gamma^2}{2\gamma-1}$$ The rest of the argument follows similarly, with $\bar{C}_2(\gamma)=\max\left\{1,C_p(1+2\pi \bar{C}_1(\gamma))\right\}$, $\bar\Psi(q)=\max \left\{1,\left(\int_{\partial\Omega}|w|^q\right)^{\frac1q}\right\}$, and $\bar \Psi(2p\gamma)\le (\bar C_2(\gamma))^{\frac{1}{2\gamma}}\bar \Psi(2\gamma)$, starting the iteration at $2\gamma=p_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Hypothesis (5.x) makes the constants uniform, so the iteration starts at $2\gamma=p_0$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.17
nodes.statement: This is a consequence of Lemma 2.3 from \cite{Cabre-SolaMorales:layer-solutions}, using definition \ref{defi-weak-solution} for weak solutions.
nodes.statement_short: Direct consequence of the cited regularity lemma applied to the weak formulation.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 5.18
nodes.statement: We apply the previous proposition to every ball $B_R(x_0,0)$, $x_0\in\mathbb R$, as in Lemma 2.3, part (b) of \cite{Cabre-SolaMorales:layer-solutions}. It uses the condition that $u$ is uniformly bounded on $\Omega$, which in our case follows from Corollary \ref{cor-Moser}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the local regularity proposition at every boundary point, using the uniform $L^\infty$ bound.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement:
Let $W$ be a potential satisfying hypothesis \emph{Ai)}. Theorem ef{thm-layer-solutions} shows existence, regularity, uniqueness and asymptotic behavior of a layer solution $0<u_W<1$ satisfying $u_W(0,0)=1/2$, $u\in\mathcal C^{2, eta}_{\mbox{loc}}(\overline{\Omega})$, for the problem  egin{equation} \left\{ egin{split} \Delta u &= 0 &\quad \mbox{in } \Omega,\  rac{\partial u}{\partial 
u} &= -W'(u) &\quad \mbox{on } \partial\Omega. \end{split}ight.\end{equation} We denote its trace value by $\phi:=u_W(\cdot,0)$. The aim of the next paragraphs is to show the more precise estimate \eqref{eq::6} for the asymptotic behavior near infinity.\ Set $a=1/\alpha$, where $\alpha=W''(0)$ as defined in (ef{eq::900}), and choose the model layer solution $u^a$ as given in \eqref{model-layer}. We know explicitly because of \eqref{asymptotic-layer} that $\phi^a:=u^a(\cdot,0)$ has the right asymptotic behavior \eqref{eq::6}. We would like to compare $u_W$ to $u^a$, in order to obtain the analogous estimate for $u_W$. Therefore, we set $v:=u_W-u^a$. Then $v$ satisfies  egin{equation*}\left\{ egin{split} &\Delta v= \;0 \quad &\mbox{in } \Omega,\ & rac{\partial v}{\partial 
u}= -W'(\phi)+V'_a(\phi^a)\quad &\mbox{on } \partial\Omega. \end{split}ight. \end{equation*} Now we estimate $$-W'(\phi)+W'(\phi^a)=-W''(0)[\phi-\phi^a]+O\lp  rac{1}{1+\abs{x}^2}p,$$ thanks to the growth estimate \eqref{growth-not-sharp}. And also, $$-W'(\phi^a)+V'_a(\phi^a)=[-W''(0)+V_a''(0)]\phi^a+O\lp  rac{1}{1+\abs{x}^2}p.$$ Because of the choice of $a$, we have that $W''(0)=V_a''(0)$. Thus adding the previous two lines we conclude that $v$ is a solution of  egin{equation*}\left\{ egin{split} &\Delta v = 0 \quad &\mbox{ in } \Omega,\ & rac{\partial v}{\partial 
u} +W''(0) v=M(x) &\mbox{ on }\partial\Omega, \end{split}ight.\end{equation*} for some function $M$ satisfying $$\abs{M(x)}=O\lp  rac{1}{1+\abs{x}^2}p .$$ Therefore, \eqref{eq::6} follows from Corollary ef{cor-comparison} (comparison principle for smooth solutions) and the fact that $W''(0)>0$. The proof of Theorem ef{th::5} is completed due to the fact that a smooth, bounded solution $u$ of \eqref{smooth-solution}, with trace $\phi$, is a viscosity solution in the sense of Definition ef{defi::1} of $$L \phi -W'(\phi)=0\quad \mbox{in }\mathbb R,$$ with $L$ defined through the L'evy-Khintchine formula, as it is noted in Lemma ef{lemma-equivalence}.
nodes.statement_short: Compare the layer $u_W$ with the explicit arctangent layer $u^a$ tuned so that $W''(0)=V_a''(0)$, then apply Corollary 5.13.

nodes.name: Import existence and regularity of the layer solution
nodes.statement: Let $W$ be a potential satisfying hypothesis \emph{Ai)}. Theorem \ref{thm-layer-solutions} shows existence, regularity, uniqueness and asymptotic behavior of a layer solution $0<u_W<1$ satisfying $u_W(0,0)=1/2$, $u\in\mathcal C^{2,\beta}_{\mbox{loc}}(\overline{\Omega})$, for the problem \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{split} \Delta u &= 0 &\quad \mbox{in } \Omega,\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial \nu} &= -W'(u) &\quad \mbox{on } \partial\Omega. \end{split}\right.\end{equation} We denote its trace value by $\phi:=u_W(\cdot,0)$. The aim of the next paragraphs is to show the more precise estimate \eqref{eq::6} for the asymptotic behavior near infinity.
nodes.statement_short: Quote Theorem 5.10 for existence, uniqueness and regularity of $u_W$.

nodes.name: Compare with the explicit model layer $u^a$
nodes.statement: Set $a=1/\alpha$, where $\alpha=W''(0)$ as defined in (\ref{eq::900}), and choose the model layer solution $u^a$ as given in \eqref{model-layer}. We know explicitly because of \eqref{asymptotic-layer} that $\phi^a:=u^a(\cdot,0)$ has the right asymptotic behavior \eqref{eq::6}. We would like to compare $u_W$ to $u^a$, in order to obtain the analogous estimate for $u_W$. Therefore, we set $v:=u_W-u^a$. Then $v$ satisfies \begin{equation*}\left\{\begin{split} &\Delta v= \;0 \quad &\mbox{in } \Omega,\\ &\frac{\partial v}{\partial \nu}= -W'(\phi)+V'_a(\phi^a)\quad &\mbox{on } \partial\Omega. \end{split}\right. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Set $a=1/\alpha$ and study the difference $v:=u_W-u^a$.

nodes.name: Linearize the boundary condition for $v$
nodes.statement: Now we estimate $$-W'(\phi)+W'(\phi^a)=-W''(0)[\phi-\phi^a]+O\lp \frac{1}{1+\abs{x}^2}\rp,$$ thanks to the growth estimate \eqref{growth-not-sharp}. And also, $$-W'(\phi^a)+V'_a(\phi^a)=[-W''(0)+V_a''(0)]\phi^a+O\lp \frac{1}{1+\abs{x}^2}\rp.$$ Because of the choice of $a$, we have that $W''(0)=V_a''(0)$. Thus adding the previous two lines we conclude that $v$ is a solution of \begin{equation*}\left\{\begin{split} &\Delta v = 0 \quad &\mbox{ in } \Omega,\\ &\frac{\partial v}{\partial \nu} +W''(0) v=M(x) &\mbox{ on }\partial\Omega, \end{split}\right.\end{equation*} for some function $M$ satisfying $$\abs{M(x)}=O\lp \frac{1}{1+\abs{x}^2}\rp .$$
nodes.statement_short: Taylor expand both potentials; the choice of $a$ cancels the leading terms, leaving $M=O(1/(1+x^2))$.

nodes.name: Apply the comparison corollary to get the sharp decay
nodes.statement: Therefore, \eqref{eq::6} follows from Corollary \ref{cor-comparison} (comparison principle for smooth solutions) and the fact that $W''(0)>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Corollary 5.13 yields the quadratic decay estimate (3.2).

nodes.name: Identify the smooth solution with a viscosity solution
nodes.statement: The proof of Theorem \ref{th::5} is completed due to the fact that a smooth, bounded solution $u$ of \eqref{smooth-solution}, with trace $\phi$, is a viscosity solution in the sense of Definition \ref{defi::1} of $$L \phi -W'(\phi)=0\quad \mbox{in }\mathbb R,$$ with $L$ defined through the L\'evy-Khintchine formula, as it is noted in Lemma \ref{lemma-equivalence}.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.6 upgrades the smooth boundary-reaction solution to a viscosity solution.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.1
nodes.statement: As we have noted in Theorem \ref{th::3}, the trace of functions in $H$ is a well defined function in $H^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb R)$. In particular, the trace mapping $T:H\to L^2(\mathbb R)$ is continuous by Sobolev embedding (Theorem \ref{Sobolev}). Then, if we have a sequence $\{u_k\}_{k=1}^\infty\to u_0$ in $H$ with $u_k\in H_0$, then $$\abs{\int_{\partial\Omega} \phi'(u_k-u_0)}\leq \lp\int_{\partial\Omega} \phi'^2\rp^{1/2} \lp\int_{\partial\Omega} \abs{u_k-u_0}^2\rp^{1/2}\to 0\quad\mbox{when } k\to \infty,$$ using the bounds for $\phi'$ given in \eqref{asymptotics}. We conclude that $u_0\in H_0$, and the lemma is shown.
nodes.statement_short: Continuity of the trace plus Cauchy-Schwarz shows the orthogonality constraint passes to the limit.

nodes.name: Continuity of the trace map into $L^2$
nodes.statement: As we have noted in Theorem \ref{th::3}, the trace of functions in $H$ is a well defined function in $H^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb R)$. In particular, the trace mapping $T:H\to L^2(\mathbb R)$ is continuous by Sobolev embedding (Theorem \ref{Sobolev}).
nodes.statement_short: $T:H\to L^2(\R)$ is continuous by the trace theorem and Sobolev embedding.

nodes.name: Cauchy-Schwarz bound along a converging sequence
nodes.statement: Then, if we have a sequence $\{u_k\}_{k=1}^\infty\to u_0$ in $H$ with $u_k\in H_0$, then $$\abs{\int_{\partial\Omega} \phi'(u_k-u_0)}\leq \lp\int_{\partial\Omega} \phi'^2\rp^{1/2} \lp\int_{\partial\Omega} \abs{u_k-u_0}^2\rp^{1/2}\to 0\quad\mbox{when } k\to \infty,$$ using the bounds for $\phi'$ given in \eqref{asymptotics}.
nodes.statement_short: The pairing with $\phi'$ passes to the limit since $\phi'\in L^2$.

nodes.name: Conclude closedness
nodes.statement: We conclude that $u_0\in H_0$, and the lemma is shown.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $u_0\in H_0$ and $H_0$ is closed.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 6.3
nodes.statement_short: Interpolate the lower bound of Lemma 6.2 with a fraction $\mu$ of $Q$ itself.

nodes.name: Convex combination of the two lower bounds
nodes.statement: It easily follows from Lemma \ref{lem:1}. Indeed, \begin{equation*} \begin{split} B(u,u) & =\int_\Omega \abs{\nabla u}^2+\int_{\partial\Omega}W''(\phi)u^2\geq (1-\mu) C_0 \int_{\partial\Omega} u^2+\mu Q(u)\\ & \geq \mu\int_\Omega \abs{\nabla u}^2+\int_{\partial\Omega} u^2\left[(1-\mu)C_0+\mu W''(\phi)\right].\\ \end{split}\end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Write $B(u,u)$ as a $\mu$-weighted combination of $Q(u)$ and the $L^2$ bound.

nodes.name: Choose $\mu$ small and conclude
nodes.statement: Because $W''$ is bounded, there exists $\mu>0$ small enough such that $(1-\mu)C_0+\mu W''(\phi)>\tfrac{C_0}{2}$. Therefore, \begin{equation} B(u,u)\geq\min\left\{\mu,\tfrac{C_0}{2}\right\} \norm{u}_H^2, \end{equation} as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Boundedness of $W''$ allows a $\mu$ making the boundary coefficient positive.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.2
nodes.statement_short: Direct method: minimize $Q$ on the constrained set, derive the Euler-Lagrange equation, and rule out a zero multiplier by a sliding-barrier comparison argument.

nodes.name: Step 1: Stability of the layer solution
nodes.statement: \emph{Step 1: Stability.} Because of the construction of $u_W$ and $\phi$, we know from Theorem \ref{thm-layer-solutions} that $Q(u)\geq 0$ for all $u\in \mathcal C_c^\infty(\bar\Omega)$ (i.e. layer solutions are stable). Thus the functional $Q$ is bounded from below also in $H$.
nodes.statement_short: Stability of layer solutions gives $Q\ge 0$ on $\mathcal C_c^\infty$, hence $Q$ is bounded below on $H$.

nodes.name: Step 2.1: Preliminaries and weak limit of a minimizing sequence
nodes.statement_short: Split $Q=Q_1+Q_2$ with $Q_1$ coercive and $Q_2$ compactly supported, then extract a weak limit $u_0$.

nodes.name: Step 2.2, Case A: $u_0\equiv0$ is impossible
nodes.statement: \emph{Step 2.2: Concluding.}\\ \emph{Case A: $u_0\equiv 0$}\\ Remark first that $$Q_1(u_k)\ge \tau \int_{\partial \Omega} u_k^2 = \tau >0.$$ On the other hand, we have $Q_2(u_k)\to Q_2(u_0)=0$. Therefore we get $$\liminf_{k\to\infty} Q(u_k) = \liminf_{k\to\infty} \left\{Q_1(u_k)+ Q_2(u_k)\right\} \ge \tau >0,$$ which is in contradiction with (\ref{eq::910}). Therefore only the next case occurs.
nodes.statement_short: If $u_0\equiv0$ then $\liminf Q(u_k)\ge\tau>0$, contradicting the assumption.

nodes.name: Step 3: Euler-Lagrange equation and the multipliers
nodes.statement: \emph{Step 3: Euler-Lagrange equation.} Once the minimizer $u_0$ is found, the theory of Lagrange multipliers for minimization problems (see, for instance, \cite{Evans}, chapter 8.4) gives that $u_0\in H$ must be a weak solution of \beB(u_0,v)=\lambda \int_{\partial\Omega} u_0v+\mu \int_{\partial\Omega} \phi'v \quad \mbox{ for every } v\in H,\ee where $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R$. The value of the multipliers can be found by choosing the right test function $v$. Thus if we test the equality \eqref{Lagrange} with $v=P*_x\phi'$, we obtain $\mu=0$ (see Lemma \ref{properties}), while testing against $v=u_0$ gives that \be\lambda=Q(u_0)=\int_{\Omega}\abs{\nabla u_0}^2+\int_{\partial\Omega} W''(\phi)u_0^2 \quad (\geq 0).\ee
nodes.statement_short: Lagrange multipliers give $B(u_0,v)=\lambda\int u_0v+\mu\int\phi'v$ with $\mu=0$ and $\lambda=Q(u_0)$.

Then, Proposition ef{prop-regularity} assures that $u_0\in\mathcal C^{1, eta}_{\mbox{loc}}( ar\Omega)$, with the following boundary estimate $$

nodes.statement_short: Moser iteration and the regularity proposition give $u_0\in\mathcal C^{1,\beta}_{loc}(\bar\Omega)$.

nodes.name: Step 5: Positivity, i.e. $\lambda\neq0$
nodes.statement: \emph{Step 5: Positivity.} In the following we show that if $\lambda=0$, then $w_0=Tu_0$ must necessarily be a multiple of $\phi'$, which is a contradiction with the fact that $u_0\in H_0$ and $\int_{\partial \Omega} u_0^2=1$. Thus we take $\lambda=0$ in \eqref{Lagrange}. Then we have a solution $u_0$ satisfying $B(u_0,v)=0$ for all $v\in H$. We remind the reader that have defined $u_W$ to be the layer solution for our potential $W$, with trace $\phi:=u_W(\cdot,0)$, and $\bar u:=\partial_x u_W$, which is also uniformly bounded and has trace $\bar u(\cdot, 0)=\phi'$. Because of the hypothesis on the potential $W$ and the asymptotic behavior of the layer solution $\phi$, there exists some $\tau>0$ such that $W''(\phi)\geq \tau$ on $\mathbb R\backslash[-R,R]$ for some $R>0$. We have shown, in particular, that $u_0$ is uniformly bounded in $\overline{\Omega}$. Since $\bar u$ is positive from \eqref{derivative-positive}, then there exists $\kappa\geq 0$ such that $\abs{u_0}<\kappa \bar u$ in $B^+_R$. We set $v:=\kappa \bar u-u_0$, and note that $v$ satisfies the conditions of Proposition \ref{prop-weak-comparison}. Thus we can conclude that $v\geq 0$ in $\overline{\mathbb R^2_+}$ so that $u_0\leq\kappa\bar u$. An analogous argument gives that $-u_0<\kappa\bar u$. We have proved that $\abs{u_0}<\kappa\bar u$ on $\overline{\mathbb R^2_+}$ and, in particular, $\abs{w(x)}<\kappa\phi'(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb R$.\\ The next step is to decrease $\kappa$ up to the first point where $\kappa\bar u$ touches $\abs{u_0}$: assume, without loss of generality, that for some $\kappa^*\geq 0$ there exists $(x_0,y_0)\in\overline{\mathbb R^2_+}$ such that \be\kappa^* \bar u=u_0 \quad \mbox{at }(x_0,y_0)\quad \mbox{and}\quad \kappa^*\bar u \ge u_0 \quad \mbox{on}\quad \overline{\Omega}.\ee We set $d_1:=\max\{W''(\phi),\tau\}$, and $d_2:=d_1-W''(\phi)$. We note that both are non-negative functions on $\mathbb R$ and $d_1(x)\geq \tau$ for all $x\in\mathbb R$. Let $v:=\kappa^*\bar u-u_0\ge 0$, that is a weak supersolution of \begin{equation*}\left\{\begin{split} &\Delta v = 0 \quad &\mbox{ in } \Omega,\\ &\frac{\partial v}{\partial \nu} +d_1 v=d_2 v \geq 0\quad &\mbox{ on }\partial\Omega. \end{split}\right.\end{equation*} We are in the hypothesis of Lemma \ref{lema-comparison}, that can be applied because the functions have enough regularity (in particular $v\in\mathcal C^{1,\beta}_{\mbox{loc}}(\overline\Omega)$). However, because of \eqref{functions-touch} we necessarily must have $v\equiv 0$. We have shown that $u_0\equiv\kappa^*\bar u$, which at the boundary translates as $w\equiv\kappa^*\phi'$.
nodes.statement_short: Slide the barrier $\kappa\bar u$ down onto $u_0$; the strong comparison principle forces $u_0\equiv\kappa^*\bar u$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Step 6: Conclusion
nodes.statement: \emph{Step 6: Conclusion.} The multiplier $\lambda$ in \eqref{eq::100} must be non-negative. However, we have shown that $\lambda\neq 0$, so then \be Q(u)\geq Q(u_0)=\lambda=: C_0>0 \quad\mbox{for all }u\in H_0 \mbox{ with }\int_{\partial\Omega} u^2=1.\ee Finally, substituting $$u_1:=\frac{u}{\sqrt{\int_{\partial\Omega} u^2}}$$ for any $u\in H_0$ into \eqref{eq:100} finishes the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:1}.
nodes.statement_short: Set $C_0:=\lambda>0$ and homogenize by normalizing $u$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6.4
nodes.statement: Note that $u_0\in H$ so, in particular, $\psi\in H^\half(\mathbb R)$ (and is also in all $L^p(\mathbb R)$ for $p>1$).\\ \emph{Claim 1:} $\psi$ is bounded; as a consequence, also $u_0$. This follows from Corollary \ref{cor-Moser}, after estimating the norm of $g$. We use the asymptotic behavior and boundedness of $\phi,\phi'$ from Theorem \ref{th::5}, and the H\"{o}lder regularity of $W''$. Then $$\int_{\mathbb R} \abs{g}^{p}\leq \int_{(-R,R)} c^{p}+\int_{\mathbb R\backslash (-R,R)} \frac{c^{p}}{\abs{x}^{p\beta}}\leq c^{p}\left[ 2R+\frac{2}{(p\beta-1)R^{p\beta-1}}\right].$$ In particular, for $R=1$, and $p>\frac{1}{\beta}$ we have, $$\norm{g}_{L^{p}(\mathbb R)}\leq K c.$$ \emph{Claim 2: } $\mathcal C^{1,\beta}_{\mbox{loc}}(\mathbb R)$ regularity for $\psi$ follows from Proposition \ref{prop-regularity}, while the uniform bound for $\psi'$ is a consequence of Corollary \ref{cor-regularity}. For the values of $\psi$ at infinity, just note that $\psi$ is a smooth function in $L^2(\mathbb R)$.
nodes.statement_short: Estimate $\|g\|_{L^p}$ uniformly to get boundedness by Corollary 5.16, then invoke the regularity results.

nodes.name: Membership of $\psi$ in $H^{1/2}$ and all $L^p$
nodes.statement: Note that $u_0\in H$ so, in particular, $\psi\in H^\half(\mathbb R)$ (and is also in all $L^p(\mathbb R)$ for $p>1$).
nodes.statement_short: $u_0\in H$ gives $\psi\in H^{1/2}(\R)\subset L^p$ for $p>1$.

nodes.name: Claim 1: boundedness of $\psi$
nodes.statement: \emph{Claim 1:} $\psi$ is bounded; as a consequence, also $u_0$. This follows from Corollary \ref{cor-Moser}, after estimating the norm of $g$. We use the asymptotic behavior and boundedness of $\phi,\phi'$ from Theorem \ref{th::5}, and the H\"{o}lder regularity of $W''$. Then $$\int_{\mathbb R} \abs{g}^{p}\leq \int_{(-R,R)} c^{p}+\int_{\mathbb R\backslash (-R,R)} \frac{c^{p}}{\abs{x}^{p\beta}}\leq c^{p}\left[ 2R+\frac{2}{(p\beta-1)R^{p\beta-1}}\right].$$ In particular, for $R=1$, and $p>\frac{1}{\beta}$ we have, $$\norm{g}_{L^{p}(\mathbb R)}\leq K c.$$
nodes.statement_short: A uniform $L^p$ bound on $g$ lets Corollary 5.16 apply.

nodes.name: Claim 2: regularity and decay of $\psi$
nodes.statement: \emph{Claim 2: } $\mathcal C^{1,\beta}_{\mbox{loc}}(\mathbb R)$ regularity for $\psi$ follows from Proposition \ref{prop-regularity}, while the uniform bound for $\psi'$ is a consequence of Corollary \ref{cor-regularity}. For the values of $\psi$ at infinity, just note that $\psi$ is a smooth function in $L^2(\mathbb R)$.
nodes.statement_short: Regularity results give $\mathcal C^{1,\beta}_{loc}$ and a uniform bound on $\psi'$.

nodes.name: Conclusion of the proof of Theorem 3.2
nodes.statement: Finally, a weak solution $\psi\in H^\half(\mathbb R)\cap \mathcal C^{1,\beta}_{\mbox{loc}}(\mathbb R)\cap L^\infty (\R)$ of \eqref{eq:20} is actually a viscosity solution of the equation \eqref{eq::7}, thus completing the proof of Theorem \ref{th::6}. This is so because of Lemma \ref{lemma-equivalence}.
nodes.statement_short: The regular weak corrector is a viscosity solution by the equivalence lemma, finishing Theorem 3.2.
